\chapter{The Sentence Learns to End}
\label{ch:ur-script-copula}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write gol he in the positions a word needs, write bari ye and nun ghunna, read hai, main, hain, nahin, maan and kahan off the page, and write mera naam ... hai from dictation.}

Three letters land on top of the seven, and the copula hai comes off the page -- with it every sentence the reader already knew how to end, including mera naam ... hai, the first sentence the book ever gave them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yih]{\ur{یہ} — \textquotedblleft{}this,\textquotedblright{} and the letter you are owed}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-yih}



\begin{quote}
Read these off the page, naming the letters from the right before you say each word:

\begin{quote}
\ur{کان}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ناک}
\end{quote}

\textbf{kān} — ear. \textbf{nāk} — nose. Seven letters bought you those.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ}} — \emph{yih} — \textbf{this}
\end{quote}

Point at something within reach and name it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{کان}} — \emph{yih kān} — \textquotedblleft{}this ear\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{ناک}} — \emph{yih nāk} — \textquotedblleft{}this nose\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two letters, and you can read the first of them: \textbf{\ur{ی}}, the S-curve with no dots. The second is new to your eye, and it will stay new for two more lessons. Say the word now; you will write it shortly.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{یہ}} points at what is \textbf{near} you. Urdu keeps a second word for what is \textbf{far}, and the two arrived together: both descend from the Old Indo-Aryan demonstratives that Sanskrit wrote as \emph{iyam} and \emph{asau}. English lost most of that system and kept a thinner \textbf{this}/\textbf{that}; Urdu kept the pair intact.

There is a gap in what you can do with \textbf{\ur{یہ}} so far, and it is worth naming. \emph{yih kān} is \textquotedblleft{}this ear\textquotedblright{} — a label, not yet a sentence. To say \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{this is} an ear\textquotedblright{} you need the small word \emph{hai} at the end, which you have been saying since you gave your name. You cannot write \emph{hai} yet, because both of its letters are still missing from your hand.

That is what this chapter buys back.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yih} — this
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yih kān}, then \textbf{yih nāk}, pointing each time
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کان} and \ur{ناک}, naming their letters from the right
  \item \emph{Say it:} the near word \textbf{yih}, and name what it still needs to become a sentence — \emph{hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this ear.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{yih kān}.) Which of \textbf{\ur{یہ}}'s two letters can you already write? (The first one, \textbf{\ur{ی}}.) What small word would turn \emph{yih kān} into a full sentence? (\emph{\textbf{hai}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DB\%8C\%DB\%81}{Wiktionary: \ur{یہ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kām]{\ur{کام} — \textquotedblleft{}work,\textquotedblright{} and a word you can read the moment you meet it}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-kaam}



\begin{quote}
Say the near-pointing word, then point at your own ear and use it. (\emph{yih}; \emph{yih kān}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کام}} — \emph{kām} — \textbf{work}
\end{quote}

Now do something you could not do with any word before this one. \textbf{Read it off the page.} From the right: \textbf{\ur{ک}}, \textbf{\ur{ا}}, \textbf{\ur{م}}.

Every letter in it is already yours, so this word arrives readable on the day you meet it. That is what the seven letters were for.

\textbf{\ur{کام}} is masculine.

\begin{quote}
\emph{yih kām} — \textquotedblleft{}this work\textquotedblright{} — the near-pointing word is still an ear-word; its second letter reaches your hand next lesson
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کام}} is \textbf{inherited}, not borrowed: Sanskrit \emph{karman} \textquotedblleft{}act, deed, work\textquotedblright{} became Prakrit \emph{kamma} and then Urdu \emph{kām}, losing a syllable to a few thousand years of being said out loud.

Then look at what English did with the same word. English did not inherit it — English \textbf{borrowed} it, late, out of books, and borrowed it whole: \textbf{karma}.

So one Sanskrit word reached two languages by two roads. The road through ordinary Indian speech wore it down to a plain word for the work you have to get done today. The road through scholarship carried it into English untouched and left it meaning cosmic consequence. Same word. The difference in weight is the difference between being inherited and being borrowed, and you have watched that same fork before, when \emph{pūchhnā} met \emph{pursish}.

A caution worth keeping: Urdu has a \textbf{second} \emph{kām}, from Sanskrit \emph{kāma} \textquotedblleft{}desire,\textquotedblright{} and it is a different word wearing the same clothes. This chapter means the working one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کام} — name the three letters from the right, then say it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kām} — work; then \textbf{yih kām}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{کام} — three letters, right to left, letting the line fall
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{kām} $\leftarrow$ Prakrit \emph{kamma} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{karman} $\to$ borrowed into English as \textbf{karma}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name \textbf{\ur{کام}}'s three letters from the right. (\textbf{\ur{ک،} \ur{ا،} \ur{م}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}this work.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{yih kām}.) Which road shortened the word, the inherited one or the borrowed one? (\textbf{The inherited one.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%A9\%D8\%A7\%D9\%85}{Wiktionary: \ur{کام}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gol he]{\ur{ہ} — the round he, and its four faces}

\label{lesson:UR-W17-he}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{کام} and say it. Three letters, right to left, the line falling as it goes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ہ}
\end{quote}

Standing on its own it is \textbf{one small closed loop} with a short curved tail falling away to the left. Draw the loop clockwise from the top, then let the tail drop. Its name is \textbf{\ur{ہ}} \emph{gol he} — \textquotedblleft{}round he\textquotedblright{} — and it says \textbf{h}.

Joining \textbf{trims} a letter, you were told. Gol he is where that promise gets tested, because it changes more than any letter you have written. Four positions, four faces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{standing alone}, and at the \textbf{end} of a word after a non-joining letter: the small loop with its tail
  \item \textbf{opening} a word: the loop stays, the tail is cut short so the next letter can begin
  \item \textbf{in the middle}: the loop splits into \textbf{two small loops side by side}, low on the line
  \item \textbf{closing} a joined word: the loop flattens into a single round curl hanging off the letter before it
\end{itemize}

The middle form is the one to look at twice. It does not resemble the standing loop at all, and a reader who knows only the standing form meets it mid-word and thinks a new letter has arrived. Same letter, doing its middle job.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Three words, one letter, three positions. Read each from the right, then copy it while the model is still in front of you.

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہم}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کہانی}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{ہم}} \emph{ham} \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} — gol he \textbf{opens} it, tail trimmed, running into \textbf{\ur{م}}. \textbf{\ur{کہانی}} \emph{kahānī} \textquotedblleft{}story\textquotedblright{} — gol he sits \textbf{in the middle}, wearing the two-loop face. \textbf{\ur{یہ}} \emph{yih} \textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{} — gol he \textbf{closes} it, and the word you were owed two lessons ago is now one you can write rather than take on trust.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہ} standing alone — the loop, then the falling tail
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{یہ} — and say \textbf{yih}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کہانی} — name its five letters, and say which face its he wears
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word can you now write that you could not before? (\textbf{\ur{یہ}}.) What sound does gol he carry? (\textbf{h}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kahāṅ]{\ur{کہاں} — \textquotedblleft{}where,\textquotedblright{} and the family it belongs to}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-kahan}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{یہ} and say it. Which face is gol he wearing there — the opening one, the middle one, or the closing one? (\textbf{Closing}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کہاں}} — \emph{kahāṅ} — \textbf{where}
\end{quote}

Four letters. Three of them are yours: \textbf{\ur{ک}}, then \textbf{\ur{ہ}} wearing its middle face, then \textbf{\ur{ا}}. The fourth is new, and it carries the nasal hum you can hear at the end of \emph{kahāṅ} — the same hum that ends \emph{maiṅ}, \emph{hūṅ} and \emph{nahīṅ}. Say the word; the letter arrives before this chapter closes.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{کہاں؟}} — \emph{yih kahāṅ?} — \textquotedblleft{}this, where?\textquotedblright{} — pointing and asking at once
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Put the question words you have met beside the new one and read down the right edge:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{کیا}} — \emph{kyā} — what
  \item \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} — \emph{kahāṅ} — where
  \item \emph{kaun} — who
  \item \emph{kab} — when
  \item \emph{kaise} — how
\end{itemize}

Every one of them opens with \textbf{\ur{ک}}. That shared consonant is not a coincidence and not a tidy invention: it is inherited. All five come from the Old Indo-Aryan interrogative stem \emph{ka-}, and \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} in particular runs back through Prakrit \emph{kahiṅ} to Sanskrit \emph{kasmin}, \textquotedblleft{}in what.\textquotedblright{}

Now say the English list out loud — \emph{who, what, when, where, how} — and listen for its own shared opening. English marks its questions with \textbf{wh}, Latin marks them with \textbf{qu} in \emph{quis} and \emph{quid}, and Urdu marks them with \textbf{\ur{ک}}. Three marks, one inherited consonant: Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}is}, split three ways by three sound histories.

So a learner meeting \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} is not memorising an arbitrary shape. They are meeting a relative of the word they already use for the same job.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kahāṅ} — where; then \textbf{yih kahāṅ?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the five k- question words — \textbf{kyā, kahāṅ, kaun, kab, kaise}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کیا} and \ur{کہاں}, naming their letters from the right
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{kahāṅ} $\leftarrow$ Prakrit \emph{kahiṅ} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{kasmin} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}is} $\to$ English \textbf{where}, Latin \textbf{quis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}where.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{kahāṅ}.) How many of its four letters can you already write? (\textbf{Three.}) Name two other members of its k- family. (\textbf{kyā, kaun, kab, kaise} — any two.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%A9\%DB\%81\%D8\%A7\%DA\%BA}{Wiktionary: \ur{کہاں}}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[baṛī ye]{\ur{ے} — the big ye, and the end of the sentence}

\label{lesson:UR-W17-bari-ye}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ی}, then \ur{ہ}. One is an S-curve that hooks up at the tip; the other is a small loop with a falling tail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ے}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{wide, flat sweep}. Start high on the right, drop through a long shallow curve that goes \textbf{well below the baseline}, and carry it a long way to the left, finishing \textbf{flat} — with no hook, no lift at the tip, and no dots.

Its name is \textbf{\ur{ے}} \emph{baṛī ye}, \textquotedblleft{}big ye,\textquotedblright{} and the letter you already know, \textbf{\ur{ی}}, is \emph{choṭī ye}, \textquotedblleft{}small ye.\textquotedblright{} Two names, one family, and one test that separates them at a glance:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{ی}} \emph{choṭī ye} is narrow and \textbf{curls back up} at its tip
  \item \textbf{\ur{ے}} \emph{baṛī ye} is broad and \textbf{runs out flat}
\end{itemize}

There is a second difference, and it is about where each one lives. Small ye turns up anywhere in a word — opening it, in the middle, closing it. Big ye belongs to the \textbf{end of a word} and turns up nowhere else, which means you will never have to work out its middle face. It has none.

Big ye carries a final \textbf{e} or \textbf{ai} sound.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Two letters, and the smallest word in Urdu that does real work:

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہے}
\end{quote}

From the right: \textbf{\ur{ہ}}, then \textbf{\ur{ے}}. Say it: \textbf{hai} — \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}

That is the word you have been putting at the end of your sentences since you first said your name, and it has been sitting on the page unreadable for sixteen chapters. Read it now.

Two more, both already in your ear:

\begin{quote}
\ur{کیسے}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کالے}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{کیسے}} \emph{kaise} — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} with small ye in the middle and big ye at the end, so the pair sit in one word and you can see the difference for yourself. \textbf{\ur{کالے}} \emph{kāle} — the masculine plural of \textquotedblleft{}black.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Nine letters. Now read the first sentence this book ever gave you, whole, with nothing taken on trust:

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے}
\end{quote}

\emph{merā nām ... hai} — \textquotedblleft{}my name is ...\textquotedblright{}. Every letter in it is one you can form: \textbf{\ur{م،} \ur{ی،} \ur{ر،} \ur{ا}} — \textbf{\ur{ن،} \ur{ا،} \ur{م}} — \textbf{\ur{ہ،} \ur{ے}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ے} — wide, flat, below the line, no hook at the tip
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہے} — and say \textbf{hai}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کیسے} — and point at the small ye and the big ye in turn
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے} — and say it with your own name in the gap
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ye curls up at the tip? (\textbf{Small ye, \ur{ی}}.) Which runs out flat? (\textbf{Big ye, \ur{ے}}.) Write \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{ہے}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māṅ]{\ur{ماں} — \textquotedblleft{}mother,\textquotedblright{} and a sentence you can read whole}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-maan}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ہے} and say it. Then write \ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے} and say it with your own name in the gap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ماں}} — \emph{māṅ} — \textbf{mother}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{ماں}} is feminine, so the possessive takes its feminine form — \emph{merī}, not \emph{merā}, the same choice you already make for \emph{bahan}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{میری} \ur{ماں} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{yih merī māṅ hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my mother.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Read that sentence off the page. Every letter in it is one you can form except the last of \textbf{\ur{ماں}}, which arrives shortly — and you can hear exactly where it goes, because it is the nasal hum you have been putting on the end of \emph{maiṅ} and \emph{hūṅ} all along.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ماں}} is \textbf{inherited}. It comes down through Prakrit from Sanskrit \emph{mātā}, stem \emph{mātṛ}, and behind that stands Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*méh\textsubscript{2}tēr}. The same root gives English \textbf{mother}, Latin \textbf{mater} (behind \emph{maternal}, \emph{matrix}), Greek \textbf{mētēr}, and Persian \textbf{mādar}.

Then notice what Urdu did with the Persian one. It took it. \emph{mādar} lives in Urdu too, alongside \emph{māṅ} — the borrowed word kept for formal, poetic and respectful use, the inherited word used at home. This is the pairing you already saw when inherited \emph{bhāī} sat beside borrowed \emph{khāndān}: Urdu rarely replaces a native word with a Persian one. It keeps both and gives them different rooms to stand in.

\textbf{*méh\textsubscript{2}tēr} also earns a caution. Words for mother across the world's languages tend to start with \emph{m}, because \emph{ma} is close to the first sound a baby makes, and that resemblance can arise anywhere without any shared ancestor. The Urdu-to-English link here is not that kind of accident — it is traceable step by step through Sanskrit and Proto-Indo-European. But a resemblance to a \emph{mama} in an unrelated family would be.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{māṅ} — mother; then \textbf{merī māṅ}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{یہ} \ur{میری} \ur{ماں} \ur{ہے۔} — name the letters of each word, then say it
  \item \emph{Say it:} the family words so far — \textbf{māṅ, bahan, bhāī, dost, khāndān}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{māṅ} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{mātā} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*méh\textsubscript{2}tēr} $\to$ English \textbf{mother}, Persian \textbf{mādar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \emph{māṅ} and \emph{mādar} you would use at home
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my mother.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{yih merī māṅ hai.}) Why \emph{merī} and not \emph{merā}? (\textbf{\ur{ماں}} is \textbf{feminine}.) Name the English cousin of \textbf{\ur{ماں}}. (\textbf{Mother}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%85\%D8\%A7\%DA\%BA}{Wiktionary: \ur{ماں}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yih merī māṅ hai]{\ur{ہے} — the smallest word, in every sentence you own}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-review-hai}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ہے}. Two letters: the small loop, then the wide flat sweep. Say it: \textbf{hai}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Four sentences. Read each from the right, word by word, and say it before you move on.

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{میری} \ur{ماں} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{کام} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{کالا} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\emph{merā nām ... hai.} — \emph{yih merī māṅ hai.} — \emph{yih kām hai.} — \emph{yih kālā hai.}

Look at what sits at the end of every one of them. \textbf{\ur{ہے}} is where an Urdu sentence lands, in the place English puts \emph{is} in the middle. You have been producing that landing by ear since the very first sentence you learned; from today you can also see it.

\subsection*{Your turn — by ear}
Page shut. Point at things around you and land each sentence on \emph{hai}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yih kām hai} — this is work
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yih merī māṅ hai} — this is my mother
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yih lāl hai}, then \textbf{yih kālā hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kahāṅ?} — and hum the nasal at its end
  \item \emph{Listen:} to \emph{hai}, \emph{haiṅ}, \emph{hūṅ} one after another, and say which is yours when you speak about yourself
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{یہ} \ur{کام} \ur{ہے۔} — three words, right to left
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہے} on its own, ten times, until the flat tail stops curling up
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \emph{māṅ} and \emph{mādar} is inherited, and which is borrowed
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \emph{kām} and English \emph{karma} was worn short, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textquotedblleft{}this is work.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{کام} \ur{ہے۔}}) Which two letters make \textbf{\ur{ہے}}? (\textbf{\ur{ہ}} and \textbf{\ur{ے}}.) Which of them can end a word and nothing else? (\textbf{\ur{ے}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nūn ghunna]{\ur{ں} — nūn with the dot taken off}

\label{lesson:UR-W17-nun-ghunna}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ن}. The deep bowl, a lift, and one dot placed low inside the curve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ں}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{same deep bowl} you drew a chapter ago, swept right to left below the baseline — and then you stop. \textbf{No lift. No dot.}

Every other letter so far was identified by what was \textbf{added} to it: nūn's dot, kāf's slash, the three teeth of sīn. This one is identified by what was \textbf{taken away}, and the taking away is the meaning. Its name is \textbf{\ur{ں}} \emph{nūn ghunna}, and \emph{ghunna} is the Urdu word for a nasal hum.

Here is the difference it makes. A dotted \textbf{\ur{ن}} is a full consonant: your tongue touches the roof of your mouth and you say \textbf{n}. A dotless \textbf{\ur{ں}} asks for no consonant at all. It tells you to send the \textbf{vowel before it} through your nose and then stop. In \emph{maiṅ} the tongue never lands.

Two more facts and the letter is yours:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{ں}} closes a word and appears nowhere else. Inside a word, that same nasal hum is carried by the ordinary dotted \textbf{\ur{ن}} — which is why \textbf{\ur{منہ}} \emph{muṅh} is spelled with a dot even though nothing in it sounds like a plain \textbf{n}.
  \item Because it ends the word, \textbf{\ur{ں}} has one shape to learn and no joined faces.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Five words, all of them already in your mouth, none of them readable until now. From the right:

\begin{quote}
\ur{میں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہیں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کہاں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ماں}
\end{quote}

\emph{maiṅ} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — \emph{haiṅ} \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nahīṅ} \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kahāṅ} \textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{} — \emph{māṅ} \textquotedblleft{}mother.\textquotedblright{}

The one to dwell on is \textbf{\ur{نہیں}}. It is the word you learned for saying no, in the very first handful of words this book gave you, and it is four letters you can now name one by one: \textbf{\ur{ن،} \ur{ہ،} \ur{ی،} \ur{ں}} — with a dotted nūn opening it and a dotless one closing it, doing two entirely different jobs in a single short word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ں} — the deep bowl, and then nothing
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{میں}, then \ur{ہیں}, then \ur{نہیں}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{maiṅ}, letting the vowel hum and keeping your tongue down
  \item \emph{Point to:} at the two nūns in \ur{نہیں} and say what each one does
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{یہ} \ur{میری} \ur{ماں} \ur{ہیں۔} — and say it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{نہیں}}.) Write \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{میں}}.) Does your tongue touch the roof of your mouth at the end of \emph{maiṅ}? (\textbf{No} — the hum goes through the nose.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — ten letters, and a sentence that comes off the page}

\label{lesson:UR-C17-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write the three letters this chapter gave you and name each one: \ur{ہ،} \ur{ے،} \ur{ں}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{Nothing new is taught here.} Read each word from the right, naming its letters before you say it:

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کام}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ماں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کہاں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{میں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہیں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہے}
\end{quote}

Then the sentences:

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{میری} \ur{ماں} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{کام} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں،} \ur{یہ} \ur{میرا} \ur{کام} \ur{نہیں} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\emph{merā nām ... hai.} — \emph{yih merī māṅ hai.} — \emph{yih kām hai.} — \emph{nahīṅ, yih merā kām nahīṅ hai.}

That last one is the first thing in this book you can read that argues back.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Three letters, and three ideas that will keep paying:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a letter can change face by position} — gol he standing as one loop and sitting in the middle of a word as two, which is the shape most likely to make a reader think a stranger has arrived
  \item \textbf{a letter can belong to one position only} — big ye and nūn ghunna both close a word and turn up nowhere else, so neither costs you a middle form
  \item \textbf{a letter can be defined by subtraction} — nūn ghunna is nūn with its dot removed, and the removal is what the letter means
\end{itemize}

And one arithmetic worth doing out loud. Seven letters gave you eight words. Three more gave you \textbf{\ur{ہے}}, and with it every sentence you already knew how to end.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Page covered. Someone says the word, or you say it to yourself from the romanization alone — then write it in Urdu without looking at a model, and only then compare.

Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hear \emph{hai}, write \textbf{\ur{ہے}}, compare
  \item hear \emph{maiṅ}, write \textbf{\ur{میں}}, compare
  \item hear \emph{nahīṅ}, write \textbf{\ur{نہیں}}, compare
  \item hear \emph{yih merī māṅ hai}, write it whole, compare and repair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many letters can you now write? (\textbf{Ten}.) Which English word is \textbf{\ur{کام}}'s borrowed twin? (\textbf{Karma}.) Which English question words share \textbf{\ur{کہاں}}'s inherited consonant? (\textbf{The wh- family} — \emph{who, what, when, where}.) Which of \textbf{\ur{ماں}} and \emph{mādar} would you say at home? (\textbf{\ur{ماں}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
